pronunciation.note: Mago is Tier 2: the romanised name is plain ASCII, and the distinctive writing lives in the scripts — Hangul 마고, Hanja 麻姑 — that an ASCII restoration cannot carry. The capitalised form Mago is the scholarly citation form.

domains.title: Mago, the Great Goddess
domains.subtitle: primordial creator and earth-shaping grandmother
domains.lead: Mago is the great goddess of Korean shamanic cosmology, honoured as Mago Halmi, the grandmother who creates and shapes the world. In the Jeju creation song the landscape is her own body: her water cuts rivers, her movements raise mountains, her skirt hems the valleys into place. To Korean folk religion she is the primordial mother whose permission opens every great ritual.

cards.name: Great Goddess
cards.desc: She stands at the head of the Jeju gut invocations, the first grandmother addressed when order must be restored.

cards.name: Cosmic Creation
cards.desc: In the changsega, the Jeju creation song, she divides sky from earth and lays out the first mountains with her own hands.

cards.name: Earth Shaper
cards.desc: Mountains, rivers, and islands are traced to her body: her urine becomes rivers, her skirt becomes ranges.

cards.name: Primordial Mother
cards.desc: She sustains life, heals disorder, and links the living household to the deep time of cosmic origins.

symbols.name: Mountains and rivers
symbols.meaning: The landscape itself, understood as the body and work of Mago.

symbols.name: Skirt
symbols.meaning: A textile image of female creative power: where her skirt settles, valleys open; where it bunches, peaks rise.

symbols.name: Gourd or vessel
symbols.meaning: A womb-like container of life and abundance associated with the great mother.

symbols.name: Serpent or dragon
symbols.meaning: A chthonic companion symbolising the creative energy of earth and water.

mythology.lead: Mago's mythology has no single canonical text. It survives in the Jeju changsega (creation song) recorded from shamans in the twentieth century, in mainland folktales of the giant grandmother, and — for her Chinese namesake Magu, the “Hemp Maiden” — in medieval Daoist literature. The strands meet in one figure: an ancient female power whose body is the land and whose patience outlasts ages.

myths.title: The Grandmother Makes the World
myths.text: In the Jeju Island creation epic known as the changsega, “Song of Creation,” preserved orally by shamans and recorded only in the twentieth century, the work of making the world falls to a grandmother. Mago Halmi — “Grandmother Mago” — takes up the labour of creation with her own body: she urinates, and her water cuts the courses of rivers; she stamps and pushes, and the earth rises into ridges and peaks; her sighs turn to wind. The song's most startling gesture is its scale: this creator is not a distant sky-father but a working woman whose bodily functions are the very tools of cosmogony. Later versions collected on the Korean mainland add the motif of her vast skirt spreading over the mountains, hemming the valleys into place. Because the text survives only in modern field recordings published in Hyun Yong-jun's collections of Korean myths, scholars treat it as an oral cosmogony of great antiquity whose written form is late. The myth's meaning is plain: the Korean landscape is a grandmother's handiwork, and the land itself remembers her.

myths.title: The Skirt That Covered the Mountains
myths.text: In a folktale told across the Korean mainland, Mago Halmi's skirt is the instrument of geography itself. The grandmother spreads the cloth over a mountain range and lifts it; where the hem settles, valleys open, and where the fabric bunches, ridges rise, and she hems the whole country into shape the way a woman hems a garment. Twentieth-century folklorists recorded the motif in many regional variants, and scholars have long noted its inner logic: textile work — women's work — becomes the model of cosmogonic work. There is no single canonical version and no ancient text to cite; the story is simply what oral tradition kept, which is precisely its authority. In one family of tellings the grandmother is so large that her body alone is the terrain: her urine becomes rivers, her sighs become wind, her shoulders become the ranges. The myth's meaning is that shaping the earth is domestic labour scaled to the sky — the mountains pressed into place by a woman's hands, and the pattern cut like a skirt.

myths.title: Magu's Fingernails and the Mulberry Sea
myths.text: The Chinese Magu (麻姑), the “Hemp Maiden,” enters literature through the Daoist biography of the immortal Wang Yuan, preserved in the Shenxian zhuan attributed to Ge Hong (fourth century) and quoted in the tenth-century compendium Taiping Guangli. Summoned to the house of the official Cai Jing, Magu appears as a girl of eighteen or nineteen in shimmering robes, with fingernails long and curved like bird claws. When Cai Jing privately wishes his back could be scratched by such claws, Wang Yuan reads his thought and has Magu do exactly that. Her greeting to Wang Yuan contains the line that made her immortal in the language: since they last met, she says, the Eastern Sea has three times turned into mulberry orchards — cang hai sang tian, “blue seas become mulberry fields,” the Chinese idiom for epochal change. The anecdote reframes the goddess as the witness of deep time: young forever, she measures the world in geological ages rather than reigns or generations.

myths.title: Mago in the Gut
myths.text: In Korean shamanic ritual (gut), the primordial grandmother is not a figure of the remote past but a present power. Shamans of Jeju and the mainland invoke Mago Halmi at the opening of major ceremonies, addressing her as the first grandmother whose permission orders the rite and whose blessing steadies the household; in the Jeju tradition the sequence of invocations descends from the highest cosmic deities toward the spirits of the local landscape, and the creation grandmothers stand near the head of that ladder. Twentieth-century scholarship — Lee Jung Young's study of Korean shamanistic ritual, Hong Tae-han's history of Korean shamanism — documented these invocations as living practice rather than fossil. Contemporary interpreters such as Helen Hye-Sook Hwang have gone further, reading the Mago tradition as the remnant of an ancient goddess-centred cosmology and building a modern “Magoism” upon it, a reading influential in feminist and ecological spirituality though debated among historians of religion. The ritual myth's meaning endures: creation was a grandmother's act, and it is renewed whenever her name is properly called.

etymology.derivation: The Hanja 麻姑 literally means "hemp maiden," a figure known in Chinese Daoist lore. In Korean folk religion the name is reinterpreted as Mago Halmi, the great grandmother creator. The native Korean element ma ("big, great") and go (an honorific for an elder woman) may reinforce this reading.

nameVariations.note: Short form used in scholarly and shamanic contexts.
Standard Korean form of the honorific.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Mago, the Hangul form is 마고 and the Hanja form is 麻姑. Hangul ‘마고’ and Hanja ‘麻姑’; the figure is widely known as Mago Halmi (마고할미) or Mago Halmeoni, "Grandmother Mago." The ASCII form mago is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Mago is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Mago sits at the intersection of Korean shamanism, Chinese Daoist folklore, and contemporary goddess spirituality. Chinese sources know Magu as an immortal associated with hemp and longevity; Korean sources transform her into a creator grandmother. Modern scholars such as Helen Hye-Sook Hwang argue that Mago represents the survival of a pan-East Asian goddess religion beneath later patriarchal traditions. The figure has also been embraced by feminist and ecological movements as a symbol of female creative power and embodied relationship with the earth.
lore.culturalLegacy: Mago is increasingly central to discussions of Korean indigenous religion, feminist theology, and environmental ethics. Her name appears in scholarly monographs, goddess spirituality networks, and cultural projects that reclaim female divine imagery. Regional festivals and shamanic rituals on Jeju and the mainland invoke Mago Halmi as a protector and creator. The figure also informs Korean diaspora identity, offering a female-centred mythic anchor distinct from the male-dominated state foundation narrative.
lore.extendedMeditation: Mago asks a different question from most creator gods: not “who made the world?” but “whose world is it?” Her answer is grandmotherly and uncompromising — the land is a relative, not a resource, and the body's ordinary labours are the true instruments of cosmogony. That matters for a name. Mago written in Hangul (마고) or Hanja (麻姑) carries script and history that ASCII cannot hold; the capitalised romanisation is a scholarly courtesy, a reminder that behind the domain name stands a goddess whom many still invoke as grandmother. To restore the name is to insist that Korean cosmogony belongs on the same shelf as Hesiod and the Eddas.

lore.archaeology: Direct material evidence for Mago Halmi is scarce — shamanic song leaves no inscriptions — but her Chinese namesake is firmly anchored in stone and ink. Mount Magu (Magu Shan) at Nancheng in Jiangxi was a recognized Daoist sacred site by the Tang dynasty, and in 771 CE the calligrapher Yan Zhenqing wrote his celebrated Magu Shan xiantan ji (“Record of the Altar of the Immortals on Mount Magu”) there, one of the most famous prose inscriptions in the Chinese calligraphic canon. From the Song dynasty onward, “Magu offering birthday wine” became a standard theme in tomb furnishings, ceramics, and painting — the immortal depicted as a young woman bearing a wine jug, often riding a deer or bluebird. In Korea the archaeology is the ritual itself: the Jeju gut, with its invocations of the creation grandmothers, is a living intangible heritage documented continuously since the twentieth century.
